# Collecting ground truth

`npm run eval` scores the model against real fares. It currently has none, and
`docs/CALIBRATION.md` says so. This is how to change that.

## The rule that matters most

**Ground truth is never generated by the model.**

It is an easy mistake to make by accident: the model is right there, it produces
plausible numbers on demand, and a corpus built from it scores perfect
calibration. Every record therefore carries an `origin`, the loader rejects any
that lacks one, and the report prints the mix.

## Three kinds of evidence, in priority order

### (a) Rider-reported actuals — `origin: "reported"`

The capture on the booking handoff. A rider comes back and says what they
actually paid. This is the only source that scales, and the only one that
reflects what real riders really book.

It is also the most biased: people who bother to report may be the ones who were
surprised. Treat a small `reported` sample as a signal about outliers rather
than about the middle.

### (b) Manual collection — `origin: "manual"`

A person opens the provider apps and records what they show, for a fixed set of
routes at fixed times. Slow, small, and the only _unbiased_ per-trip truth
available without a partner feed.

**The procedure, so two people produce comparable rows:**

1. Pick a route from the standing set below. Use the exact coordinates, not an
   address search, so the route hash is stable.
2. Open RideLens. Record `predictedMinMinor`, `predictedMaxMinor`,
   `modelVersion` and `predictedAt` from the provenance sheet — it shows all
   four.
3. Within **five minutes**, open each provider app for the same two points and
   record the fare it offers **and the pickup ETA it shows**. Five minutes
   matters: the marketplace model ticks on ~55 seconds, and an hour-old
   comparison is a different question.
4. Record the fare _before_ any promotion, credit or subscription discount. Those
   are account-specific and RideLens has never claimed to model them.
5. If a provider will not quote — no cars, outside the service area — record
   nothing for it rather than a zero.
6. Append the row to `tests/fixtures/calibration-corpus.json`.

**The standing route set.** Fixed so that repeated collection is comparable, and
chosen to span the cases the model handles differently:

| Route            | From               | To                 | Why it is in the set                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `nyc-mid-jfk`    | 40.7549, −73.9840  | 40.6413, −73.7781  | The flat fare, and the tolled crossings    |
| `nyc-short-core` | 40.7359, −73.9911  | 40.7580, −73.9855  | Short, metered, inside the congestion zone |
| `nyc-outer`      | 40.6782, −73.9442  | 40.7282, −73.7949  | No Manhattan surcharge, longer run         |
| `chi-loop-ord`   | 41.8781, −87.6298  | 41.9742, −87.9073  | A market whose fees are **not** modeled    |
| `sf-soma-sfo`    | 37.7749, −122.4194 | 37.6213, −122.3790 | Another unmodeled market, different tariff |
| `dc-dupont-dca`  | 38.9097, −77.0434  | 38.8512, −77.0402  | Unmodeled fees, short airport run          |

Collect at four times of day — roughly 08:00, 13:00, 18:00 and 23:00 local — so
the time-of-day curve is exercised rather than one point on it.

**How many.** `MIN_SAMPLES` is 20 per slice. Six routes × four times × two
providers is 48 rows per collection round, which makes the overall number
reportable after one round and per-provider numbers reportable after two.

### (c) Published aggregates — `origin: "published"`

TLC trip records, academic surge studies. These are a _distributional_ sanity
check — does the model's spread look like the real spread — and cannot be
scored against an individual prediction. The loader keeps them in the corpus
for context and `scorable()` excludes them from coverage and bias.

## The record shape

```json
{
  "origin": "manual",
  "collectedVia": "iPhone 15, Uber 3.6xx, observed in-app upfront fare",
  "collectedOn": "2026-09-26",
  "routeHash": "nyc-mid-jfk",
  "provider": "uber",
  "productId": "uberx",
  "marketId": "new-york",
  "predictedMinMinor": 7245,
  "predictedMaxMinor": 7395,
  "predictedAt": "2026-09-26T18:04:00Z",
  "modelVersion": "2026-09-25.v1",
  "actualMinor": 7680,
  "distanceMeters": 26100
}
```

`collectedVia` is free text and exists so a strange row can be traced back to
how it was taken.

## The wait is worth recording too

Every card shows a pickup wait, and until recently nothing could say whether
any of them was right. The parameters behind it were attributed to studies
nobody could locate; they are now recorded in `MODEL_PARAMS.wait` as what they
actually are — priors fitted to nothing.

Three optional fields turn a row into a wait observation as well as a fare
one:

```json
{
  "predictedWaitLowSeconds": 120,
  "predictedWaitHighSeconds": 240,
  "actualWaitSeconds": 300
}
```

`actualWaitSeconds` can be either of two things, and which one matters:

- **The ETA the provider's own app showed** at the same moment. Easy, and it
  scores the model against what a rider would have seen when deciding.
- **The wait that actually happened**, from request to the car arriving.
  Harder, and the only one that scores the model against reality.

Record which in `collectedVia`. Do not mix them in one round without saying
so — the first is systematically optimistic, because a provider's ETA is
itself a prediction.

Rows without these fields are fine and will be the majority. They score the
fare and are simply skipped by the wait summary, which keeps its own sample
count and withholds below 20 like everything else.

## Running it

```bash
npm run eval
```

Writes `docs/CALIBRATION.md`. With fewer than 20 scorable records it reports
that and stops — deliberately not an error, because making an empty corpus fail
the build would train everyone to ignore the command.

To gate a parameter change on not regressing:

```bash
EVAL_MIN_SCORE=0.412 npm run eval
```

Exits non-zero if coverage-adjusted sharpness falls below the floor. Take the
floor from the current `docs/CALIBRATION.md` before changing anything in
`model-params.ts`.

## What to do with a bad result

A bad number is the most useful output this harness has. It says what to build
next:

- **Low coverage, narrow bands** — confidently wrong. Widen first so the product
  stops lying, then fix the model.
- **High coverage, wide bands** — hedging. The bands are doing the work the
  model should.
- **Bias concentrated in one market** — that market needs its own rate card or
  fee model, which is Phase 5.3.
- **Bias concentrated at one hour** — the time-of-day curve is wrong, and
  `model-params.ts` is where to change it.
- **Misses almost all below the band** — we systematically overquote, and the
  product looks more expensive than the ride is.
